newsitem.title: USA: Russia to stop aiming missiles at Japan, boost ties.
newsitem.headline: Russia to stop aiming missiles at Japan, boost ties.

text.p: Russia, seeking to improve decades of frosty ties with Pacific neighbour Japan, will stop aiming missiles against targets there and set up a telephone hotline with Tokyo, a Japanese spokesman said on Friday.
The spokesman, speaking after a breakfast meeting between Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, also said the two leaders would hold regular summit meetings.
He said they had approved a plan to boost Japanese investment in Russia, which is still struggling to revitalise its economy after decades of Soviet-era state controls.
"The president told the premier that former Soviet missiles are still targeted at Japan, and the time has come to take Japan off the targets," the spokesman said.
The announcement about missiles is mainly of symbolic value, rather than pointing to a new policy thrust.

Yeltsin, attending his fifth summit of the Group of Seven industrial states, said last month that Russia would stop targeting missiles at NATO states. Experts said it would be relatively quick and easy easy to reprogram the computers on the missiles to change this policy again.
Japan is not a NATO member, but U.S. troops are based there.
Yeltsin, speaking before meeting Hashimoto, said he was disappointed by the state of relations between the two countries and suggested that they set up a telephone hotline to improve them.
"I propose that contacts should take various shapes, including by telephone," Yeltsin said. "Your Chancellery and the Kremlin must have a direct line."
Ties between Russia and Japan have been strained for decades by a dispute over four Pacific islands seized by the Soviet army in the final days of the Second World War.
Japan says that the islands, which it terms the Northern Territories, must be returned.
Yeltsin, aware that territorial concessions would prompt a fierce backlash from his nationalist opponents, says there is no question of returning what Russia calls the Kurile Islands.
The dispute has prevented the two states signing a formal peace treaty ending Second World War hostilities.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the territorial dispute was not an issue in the bilateral talks, which dealt with fishing rights and mutual economic cooperation, including on the Kuriles and on oil-rich Sakhalin Island.
"I think we found a common language and mutual understanding," Yastrzhembsky told reporters. "I think the solution of the fishing rights problem will be speeded up."
Asked if Hashimoto would come to Russia soon, he smiled broadly and said: "More likely than not."

The Japanese spokesman said Hashimoto's domestic political schedule was so tight that a meeting might have to take place on a weekend in the Russian Far East. Russia's Pacific port of Vladivostok is only a short flight from Japan.

In addition to the territorial dispute, Japan is reluctant to countenance Russia's goal of full membership of the G7 -- which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
The Japanese spokesman said on Friday that Russia was "not ready" to join G7 discussions on issues like finance and macro-economic policy.
